name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 27 June 1972

clue.text: Vessel crosses the bar?

blocks.note: surface reading: a sailing ship clears the sandbank at a harbour mouth
setter's reading: the vessel is also a tall beer glass, handed across the counter of a pub

explanation.surface: A sailing ship makes it over the sandbar at a harbour entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: A schooner is both a two-masted sailing ship and, in Australia, a large beer glass, so the vessel can cross a harbour bar or a pub bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a fore-and-aft rigged sailing ship and also a standard Australian beer glass served over a counter.

clue.text: One's in a sort of trance, in this case

indicators.note: a sort of something is a loose version of it, so the following word is rearranged
the first part is placed inside the rearranged word

blocks.note: the word to be rearranged
one is I, plus the 's of the possessive

explanation.surface: Someone is lying in a kind of trance in this situation.
explanation.walkthrough: Case is a container here, not a situation or a patient's case; the rearranged word is a horse's pace, split to take the inserted pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A canister is a small metal container, such as a tin for tea or film, so it is a kind of case.

clue.text: Distinction awarded initially in Rome

blocks.note: surface reading: an honour first given in ancient Rome
setter's reading: the honour is known by its initials, OM, and those two letters sit in the middle of Rome

explanation.surface: An honour that was first conferred in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Order of Merit is abbreviated OM, and R-OM-E contains those initials; nothing about the honour is Roman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Order of Merit is a British honour conferred by the monarch for exceptional service in arts, science or public life.

clue.text: Poor Baker's in an elevated state

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order
the rearranged letters are placed inside the following short word
in a down clue, elevated means raised up, so the short word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A struggling baker finds himself in a state of high excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevated state sounds like a mood, but state is a US state; elevated works on the short word only, as this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Nebraska is one of the United States, a Great Plains territory admitted to the Union in 1867.

clue.text: Debauchee going to get share in spoils?

blocks.note: a rake is a dissolute man about town
going off means leaving, departing

explanation.surface: A libertine leaves to collect his portion of the loot.
explanation.definitionFit: A rake-off is a cut or commission taken from profits, often illicitly, so a slice of the proceeds.

clue.text: Wool from some farmer in Orkney?

indicators.note: some of the words means only a part of them, a run of letters inside

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of farmer, all of in and the start of Orkney

explanation.surface: Is this wool from a Scottish island farmer?
explanation.walkthrough: Orkney is a group of islands off the north of Scotland, plausible sheep country, which is why the question mark is there.
explanation.definitionFit: Merino is a fine soft fleece from a sheep breed of Spanish origin, widely farmed in Australia.

clue.text: Victor appears to cling to love

blocks.note: to hug is to cling tightly
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: The winner seems to embrace the one he adores.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor is the first name here, not a winner: the French novelist Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo was the French novelist and poet, so his surname completes the forename given in the clue.

clue.text: Borrow hook from Vera Long, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements the letters might take

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks to borrow a hook from a woman called Vera Long.
explanation.walkthrough: Borrow is George Borrow, the English writer, and hook is evidently a misprint for book; Borrow looks like a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavengro (1851) is George Borrow's semi-autobiographical novel about Gypsy life, so it is a book by that author.

clue.text: Nymph appears so in area

indicators.note: the first word is placed inside the second

blocks.note: taken as written
so and thus both mean in this way

explanation.surface: A nymph turns up looking like this in the district.
explanation.walkthrough: Appears is only a link word joining the nymph to the wordplay, though it looks like part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Arethusa was a nymph who was changed into a spring to escape the river god Alpheus.

clue.text: She may return to take courses

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to dine is to eat a meal of several courses

explanation.surface: A woman might come back to attend a series of classes.
explanation.walkthrough: Courses suggest study, but they are courses of a meal; DINE read backwards gives ENID.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid is a woman's name, and crossword setters often define a girl's name simply by a female pronoun.

clue.text: Means being out of employment'.'

blocks.note: surface reading: an explanation that something signifies being jobless
setter's reading: money that comes out of having a job, means being one's resources

explanation.surface: A definition of being unemployed.
explanation.walkthrough: Out of employment reads as jobless, but it means arising from work; means is a noun for money, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Earned income is the tax term for wages and salary received from work, as distinct from investment returns.

clue.text: Rebuff joint offer at board meeting?

blocks.note: first meaning: to snub or deliberately ignore someone
second meaning: a cut of meat served cold at a table, the board where people meet to eat

explanation.walkthrough: Board meeting suggests directors, but a board is also a dining table, and the joint is a roast.
explanation.definitionFit: To cold-shoulder someone is to snub them, and a cold shoulder of mutton is a leftover roast served at table.

clue.text: Condescends So take work on board, apparently

indicators.note: on board a ship means inside the steamship abbreviation, which wraps the rest

blocks.note: SS stands for steamship, and what is on board goes between its letters
as printed this reads So; the original clue almost certainly read to, taken as written
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone deigns to take a job aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is garbled in this printing: it should read Condescends to take work on board, apparently; the steamship abbreviation wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To stoop is to lower oneself to do something beneath one's dignity, which is exactly condescending.

clue.text: Nonsensical measure connected with fish

blocks.note: a foot is an imperial unit of length
the ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: A silly unit of length linked to a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Footling means trivial or silly, of no importance, so a footling remark is foolish and pointless.

clue.text: Walk heavily like a character in “The Virginian”

blocks.note: to tramp is to tread with heavy steps
like and as both mean in the manner of

explanation.surface: Stomping about like a figure from a classic Western.
explanation.walkthrough: The Virginian is Owen Wister's 1902 cowboy novel, later a film and TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Trampas is the villain of The Virginian, the cattle rustler who is finally shot by the hero.

clue.text: Leaves carrier — each entering the river

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the first word sits within the second

blocks.note: the Test is a river in Hampshire, England, famous for trout fishing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A porter is departing, with each one going into the river.
explanation.walkthrough: Leaves looks like a verb meaning departs, but it is tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea chest is a light wooden box used to ship tea, so it holds and transports tea leaves.

clue.text: Eminent executant in some art form

indicators.note: to form is to shape, so the letters are given a new shape

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A distinguished performer in a particular artistic genre.
explanation.walkthrough: Art form reads as one phrase, but form is the instruction and some art is the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a distinguished musician or conductor, a masterly performer, which is what an eminent executant is.

clue.text: Vouch for the account — many tried arranging that

indicators.note: arranging means putting in a fresh order, so the word's letters are reordered

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for account
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Many people attempted to confirm the story.
explanation.definitionFit: To accredit someone is to officially recognise or certify them, giving one's authority as guarantee.

clue.text: Natural phenomenon for Henry Wiggins, plainly Spanish

blocks.clueFragment: Natural phenomenon for Henry Wiggins, plainly Spanish
blocks.note: surface reading: some feature of nature that a man named Henry finds obviously Spanish
setter's reading: the phonetics professor of My Fair Lady drills the line about weather in Spain falling mainly on the plain

explanation.surface: A man named Henry thinks some natural event is clearly Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: Wiggins stands for Henry Higgins of My Fair Lady, whose pupil recites The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain; plainly hints at the plain.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainfall is precipitation, a weather event in nature, and Higgins's famous sentence describes it on the Spanish plain.

clue.text: The poet we'd pick?

blocks.note: first meaning: Thomas ..., Elizabethan poet and songwriter
second meaning: a wild flower with pink or white blooms, something one might pick

explanation.walkthrough: We'd pick sounds like choosing a favourite poet, but it is picking flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Campion wrote lute songs around 1600, and campion is also a common hedgerow wildflower.

clue.text: The course to go to Mars, for example?

definitions.text: The course to go to Mars, for example?

blocks.clueFragment: The course to go to Mars, for example?
blocks.note: surface reading: a flight path to the red planet
setter's reading: a course of a meal, served to Mars the Roman war god, as an example of a deity

explanation.surface: Plotting the route for a spacecraft heading to Mars.
explanation.walkthrough: Mars is the god, not the planet, and course is a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia is the food of the gods in classical myth, and the name is also used for a fruit dessert course.

clue.text: Understands a point in children's pastime

blocks.note: to see is to understand, as in I see
taken as written
W is west, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone grasps the purpose of a children's game.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a plank balanced on a pivot that children ride up and down at a playground.

clue.text: Composer gets many an offer of a lift?

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many
hop in is what a driver says when offering someone a ride

explanation.surface: A composer is offered numerous rides.
explanation.definitionFit: Frédéric Chopin was the Polish Romantic composer famous for his piano nocturnes and études.

clue.text: Animal springs to view in Wordsworth's poem

blocks.note: a hart is a male deer
the plural asks for two springs: a leap is a spring through the air, a well a spring of water

explanation.surface: A deer bounds into sight in a poem by Wordsworth.
explanation.walkthrough: Springs looks like a verb for the animal, but it supplies two nouns, one for each sense of spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Hart-Leap Well is a Wordsworth ballad of 1800 about a hunted stag's last great leap beside a spring.

clue.text: Out-and-out row?

blocks.note: first meaning: utter, complete, as in a complete outsider
second meaning: a line, as of soldiers or taxis

explanation.walkthrough: Row suggests a quarrel, but it is a line; the question mark asks you to look past that.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank as an adjective means utter or downright, and as a noun it is a line of people or things.

clue.text: Give a hand in port

blocks.note: first meaning: to distribute playing cards to the players
second meaning: a harbour town on the coast of Kent, England

explanation.surface: Someone helps out at a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Give a hand sounds like helping, but the hand is a set of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal is to hand out cards for a game, and Deal is a seaside town in Kent on the English Channel.

clue.text: Capital gains to a manufacturer?

indicators.note: a manufacturer makes things, so these letters are made into something new

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Capital investment brings profits to a factory owner.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks financial, but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the capital city of Chile, at the foot of the Andes.

clue.text: Brown returns to mountains to make notes

indicators.note: something that returns goes back, so the colour word is read right to left

blocks.note: tan is a light brown
the Urals are the range dividing Europe from Asia, with to joining it on

explanation.surface: Brown goes back to the mountains to write down some observations.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown looks like a person, and notes look like jottings; they are a colour and musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a natural is a note that is neither sharp nor flat, marked by the natural sign.
